title: Act III, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: Cinna the poet, who has dreamed of feasting with Caesar, goes out to the funeral. A mob of plebeians questions him. When he gives his name, they confuse him with Cinna the conspirator; when he protests that he is the poet, they cry 'Tear him for his bad verses' and kill him anyway.

context.history: Plutarch reports that the poet Helvius Cinna was killed by a mob that mistook him for the conspirator Cornelius Cinna.

significance: This short scene shows the result of Antony's speech: a mob that no longer listens to reason. It darkly mirrors the conspirators' own violence. Note: this scene depicts mob violence; preview with students.
discussionQuestions: What happens to truth when a crowd is angry?
Where does conflict appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with power, ambition and tyranny?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show Cinna the poet? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Cinna the poet? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene III develops the idea of Cinna the poet. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of Cinna the poet. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene III suggests about Cinna the poet. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's conflict and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses conflict in Act III, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of Cinna the poet. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Cinna the poet responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Cinna the poet follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene III and its treatment of Cinna the poet. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's conflict and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about Cinna the poet in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Cinna the poet. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
